opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so for our SWE-bench work, we deliberately went with a really minimal setup. We basically gave the model a bash tool and a file-editing tool, and let it explore the repository on its own, the same way a human engineer would if you dropped them into an unfamiliar codebase. It'll run `ls`, look at the directory structure, grep for function names, open up files, read them, and gradually build up a picture of where the relevant code lives.

Part of the reasoning is that we wanted to measure the model's capability rather than the capability of the scaffolding around it. A lot of the earlier SWE-bench approaches had quite elaborate pipelines: retrieval systems, code indexing, multi-stage localization steps. Those can definitely help, but they also bake in a lot of human assumptions about how the problem should be broken down. And what we've found is that as models get smarter, those hand-engineered steps can actually start to hold the model back. If your retrieval system picks the wrong files, the model never gets a chance to recover. Whereas if the model is doing the exploration itself, it can notice "oh, this isn't quite right," backtrack, and look somewhere else.

The other thing is that letting the model explore is just more general. A code-indexing system is tuned to a particular kind of task. But bash plus an editor works for pretty much anything: debugging, writing tests, reproducing the issue first, running the test suite to check its fix. We saw the model do all of that pretty naturally. It'll often write a little reproduction script, run it, see the error, make the fix, and run it again to confirm.

The tradeoff is cost and time. Agentic exploration uses a lot more tokens than a single retrieval step, because the model might open a bunch of files that turn out not to matter. But for a benchmark like this, and honestly for a lot of real-world use, we think it's worth it. And my general bet is that the trend continues: the more capable the models get, the more you want to give them simple, flexible tools and get out of their way, rather than building complicated systems around them.

r001.rationale: It says the model can inspect what it found, recognize when the files are not right, backtrack, and search elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It says the model explores the repository and finds relevant code itself, instead of relying on a retrieval or indexing system.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the more surprising things to us. When we started working on SWE-bench, a lot of the existing approaches had this really elaborate retrieval setup — you'd embed the whole repo, build some kind of index, maybe do BM25 on top of that, and then hand the model a curated set of files that were probably relevant to the issue. And the thought was, well, the model can't read the whole codebase, so you need to pre-digest it.

And what we found was that we basically didn't need any of that. We gave the model a really simple set of tools — essentially bash, and a file editor — and we just let it go. And it turns out that if you give the model the same tools a human engineer would use, it does roughly what a human engineer would do. It greps for the error message. It finds the function that's mentioned in the issue, looks at where that's called from, opens up a couple of files, reads the tests. It navigates. It's not getting a snapshot of the repo handed to it, it's actively exploring, and it can course-correct when its first guess is wrong.

That last part is the important bit, I think. A retrieval system gives you one shot. If the index returns the wrong files, the model is kind of stuck — it either confidently edits the wrong place or it has to guess. Whereas when the model is doing the search itself, it can look at something, realize "no, this isn't it," and go search for something else. That iterative loop is where a lot of the performance comes from.

And honestly, part of why we leaned into this was a philosophy thing. Every piece of scaffolding you build around the model is an assumption about what the model can't do. And those assumptions get stale really fast. The retrieval system that helped the last generation of models becomes a bottleneck for the next one, because now you're constraining a model that could have figured it out on its own. So our bias was: keep the scaffold as minimal as possible, give the model good tools and a good environment, and put the intelligence in the model rather than in the harness. If something doesn't work, that's useful signal for what to train on, not necessarily a sign that you need to add more machinery around it.

Now, I don't want to overclaim — there are definitely cases where some kind of index could help, especially on enormous monorepos where even a smart engineer would want a map. But for SWE-bench-style repos, the model exploring on its own was simpler, more robust, and frankly it just worked better than we expected.

r001.rationale: The response says the model examines what it finds, recognizes when it is the wrong place, and searches for something else, describing an iterative search guided by results.

r002.rationale: It says the model uses tools to explore the repository and open relevant files itself, contrasting this with a system handing it a curated set of files.

astra-6.text:
I think the tradeoff is between doing retrieval up front and letting the model figure out what it needs as it goes. With an index, you’re trying to predict which pieces of code will be relevant before the model has really investigated the problem. But often, you read one file and that tells you what to look for next.

So you can give Sonnet basic tools to search the repository and read files, and let it follow that trail. Search for a symbol or an error message, inspect the surrounding code, look at who calls it, find the tests. That makes finding the relevant code part of solving the problem.

There’s a cost to that in extra tool calls, and indexing can still be useful. But I’d start with the simplest tools and see where the model actually gets stuck before building a more elaborate retrieval system.

r001.rationale: It says reading one file can guide what to look for next and describes Sonnet following that search trail.

r002.rationale: It says to let Sonnet search the repository and read files to find relevant code, contrasting this with predicting relevance using an index up front.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is how much infrastructure you actually need to put around the model. You can build a code index and try to retrieve the right snippets up front, but then you’re making a lot of decisions about what the model is going to need before it’s really investigated the problem.

The alternative is to give Sonnet tools to search the repository and read files, and let it follow the trail. It can search for something from the issue, look at the surrounding code, find the callers, and revise its hypothesis. Finding the relevant code becomes part of solving the problem.

That’s a really appealing approach for SWE-bench because you can keep the scaffolding simple. It doesn’t mean indexing can’t help, but I’d start by seeing how far the model can get with the same basic tools a developer would use, and add infrastructure where you see a concrete failure.

r001.rationale: It says Sonnet can search, inspect surrounding code and callers, then revise its hypothesis and follow the trail, communicating that search continues based on what it finds.

r002.rationale: It contrasts indexing with giving Sonnet repository search and file-reading tools so it can find relevant code itself.
